title: Fat Bear Week Returns: 16 Bears Battle for the Chubby Crown
summary:
Every autumn, millions of people stare at their screens and ask one very important question: which Alaskan brown bear is the fattest?

Welcome to Fat Bear Week, now in its 12th year. From September 22 to 29, 2026, fans worldwide vote for the chubbiest brown bear in Katmai National Park. The park spans 4.1 million acres of volcanoes, rivers, and forests — and it's home to about 2,200 brown bears. There are no roads in, so visitors arrive by boat or plane to watch the animals safely.

The contest began in 2014, when Park Ranger Mike Fitz noticed two photos of the same bear on the park's website. One was taken in June, the other in September. The difference was dramatic — the bear had packed on serious pounds. Fitz and other rangers turned the idea into a one-day Facebook event called "Fat Bear Tuesday," where votes were counted through "likes." The next year, it expanded into a full week, and it's been growing ever since. In 2025, more than 1.7 million votes were cast from over 100 countries.

How does it work? It's a single-elimination bracket, like a sports tournament. Each day, fans vote online for one of two bears in a matchup. The winner advances; the loser is eliminated. After several rounds, two bears remain. The one with the most votes on the final day is crowned champion.

This year's lineup features 16 bears and bear families, each with a story. Bear 32, known as Chunk, is back to defend his 2025 title after recovering from a broken jaw. Bear 164, or Bucky, became a fan favorite this summer for snatching leaping salmon out of the air. Bear 132 is competing while raising three cubs — one of which got separated from the family and survived alone for several days before reuniting. And Bear 806 is raising her own cub plus an adopted young bear named Biggie.

Why do bears need all that fat? It's their winter survival fuel. The contest is a fun way to follow these animals — and a reminder of why protecting their wild Alaskan home matters.

The final round is September 29. Who's your pick?
why_it_matters: Stories like this show that science and conservation can reach millions when they are wrapped in play and competition — the same habits of careful observation and evidence that decide a bracket also decide how a society protects wild places and the animals in them.

background_read: Katmai National Park (a huge protected wilderness in southwest Alaska, first set aside after a massive volcanic eruption in the early 1900s) holds one of the densest brown bear populations on Earth.
Every summer, salmon swim up the park's Brooks River to spawn, and the bears crowd the river to catch them — packing on the fat they will burn while hibernating through the long Alaskan winter.

Fat Bear Week grew out of the park's live bear cameras, streamed online by the nonprofit explore.org, which let millions of people watch the same individual bears day after day and learn to recognize them.
Ranger Mike Fitz (a park ranger who helped create the contest) compared two photos of one bear, from June and September, and saw how dramatically it had changed.

The idea has become a model for how conservation groups use humour and internet culture to pull people into wildlife science — and the weight really matters, because a bear that enters winter too thin may not survive, and a mother's cubs depend on her fat reserves too.

perspectives.description: The contest turns an invisible scientific process, winter hibernation preparation, into something millions of people follow and care about. Fans learn individual bears by name, and that attention can translate into support for protecting habitat.

Some argue that reducing wild animals to a popularity contest and joking about their weight trivialises real problems. Brown bears in Alaska still face threats from climate change, shrinking salmon runs and conflicts with humans, and a bracket of cute photos does not solve any of that.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — analysts of online science communication
perspectives.description: Fat Bear Week fits a wider pattern of wildlife brackets, citizen-science projects and live cameras that use voting to make people feel involved. It also depends heavily on a single platform partner and on the bears' salmon run happening on schedule.

If warming water and rivers affect the salmon run, the bears' autumn weight gain could weaken over time, which would show up directly in the contest. That makes each year's bracket an accidental record of how healthy the ecosystem is.
